reason: readPathValue returning 1 instead of 0 when a path segment hits a non-object changes the sort value, so a contention test with a sortBy path traversing a non-object would reorder differently.

The explicit `a.index - b.index` tiebreak on delta===0 is redundant given V8's guaranteed stable Array.sort; skipping it (returning delta=0) preserves the same input order, so no test can distinguish.
Skipping the `entity.state = {}` init when state is not a record makes line 19 dereference `undefined[key]` and throw, which a test patching an entity with missing/non-object state would catch.

For a truthy non-object physics the original returns null (logs error), while `if (false)` proceeds and isSamePosition/assignment operate on the non-object, so a test with malformed physics would observe the difference.

When ledger.incoming is a truthy non-object the original returns null but `if (false)` returns it, causing `incoming[key] = ...` to run on a primitive; a test with a malformed ledger.incoming distinguishes it.

Removing the missing-source/target guard makes calculateTransaction run with an undefined entity instead of logging and returning, so a transfer test with a nonexistent source or target id would catch it.
Forcing `if (true)` always logs the not-found error and returns, so a valid automation update is silently skipped; an uncovered test updating an existing entity's automation would fail.

Changing `||` to `&&` lets a null or truthy-non-object cave bypass the guard and be treated as a component, so a test with a null/non-object cave would observe the missing error and altered progression.
Every mergeAttributes call site guards the update argument with a truthy `?` check (baseDemand/maxDemand/allocatedDraw), so `!update` is never true and dropping the early return changes nothing.

readNumericValue returning 1 instead of 0 for a non-numeric state value shifts saturation and thus calculateHeadroom, so a clamp test with a resource whose value field is missing/non-numeric would differ.
Changing `nextAmount > 0` to `nextAmount > 1` drops clamped amounts in (0,1] from the result, so a headroom-limited transfer of a fractional or exactly-1 amount would no longer be recorded.

Flipping `!==` to `===` makes the function return early exactly when blueprintId IS a string (the normal case) and proceed otherwise, so an uncovered test with a valid unified blueprint would see no peer kills enqueued.

When source has no memberships, hasUnifiedBlueprintSharedTag({}, peer) is always false so the loop enqueues nothing; skipping the early return only iterates without side effects, yielding identical behavior.

Raising the `Math.max(0, ...)` floor to `Math.max(1, ...)` in readBodySerial makes a stored serial of 0 (or negative) read as 1, changing the next assigned bodySerial, which a test seeding bodySerial at 0 would catch.
Skipping the missing-sys_world guard makes `worldEntity.assignment ??= ...` throw on undefined instead of logging and returning null, so a test spawning a body with no sys_world entity would fail.

Forcing `if (true)` overwrites state.bodySerial even when passport.identitySerial is already set, so a test supplying a preset identitySerial and asserting the untouched world bodySerial would observe the change.

Flipping `===` to `!==` makes readBodySerial always return 0 (numbers fail the type check, non-numbers fail isFinite), so the assigned serial never increments past 1; a test spawning a second body expecting serial+1 would catch it.

Flipping self-skip `entity.id === body.id` to `!==` makes the loop skip all real other bodies and only consider the body itself, breaking overlap resolution; an uncovered test with an overlapping neighbor would see the position not adjusted.

Flipping `parent.kind === "entity_id"` to `!==` sends entity_id parents down the tag branch (and tag parents to entityId lookup), resolving the wrong or no parent; an uncovered test with an entity_id parent would get a wrong parent id.

Changing `!parent || "parentId" in parent` to `&&` makes an undefined parent hit `"parentId" in undefined` and throw, and lets a concrete parentId parent fall through instead of returning false; an uncovered peer-parent test distinguishes both.
Setting buildPhysicsBody's initial `acceleration.x` to 1 instead of 0 changes the constructed/persisted body, so a persistence test deep-comparing the physics body's acceleration would catch it.

Flipping `blueprintId === "sys_pointer"` to `!==` swaps the selected system config (pointer gets world config and vice versa), so a test spawning sys_pointer or sys_world and checking its label/tags/components would differ.

Changing `current && typeof current === "object"` to `||` makes a null final segment reach `"value" in null` and throw instead of returning 0, so a radius test with a valueRef path ending in null distinguishes it.
Returning undefined instead of the resolved number makes a direct numeric valueRef path yield NaN ratio and thus NaN physics.radius, which a test with a top-level numeric path would catch.

resolveNumericPath is only ever called with a truthy valueRef/maxRef (guarded by `if (valueRef)`/`if (maxRef)`), so `!path` never holds; and even with an empty path the entity has no top-level numeric `value`, so it still returns 0.
Flipping `min + (max - min) * clampedRatio` to `min - ...` inverts the radius interpolation, so any test with a nonzero clampedRatio (valueRef resolving above 0) would see a wrong physics.radius.
Raising the clamp ceiling from `Math.min(1, ratio)` to `Math.min(2, ratio)` lets ratios in (1,2] escape the 1-cap, so a test with valueRef exceeding maxRef (ratio>1) would compute a larger radius.

Forcing the top-level-number branch to `if (false)` makes a numeric path fall through to the object-value check and return 0 instead of the number, so a direct numeric valueRef test would see radius computed from 0.

Changing `entry.value > newMax` to `>=` triggers scaling when value equals newMax, setting value = newMax*(newMax/oldMax) below newMax instead of leaving it at newMax; an uncovered boundary test with value===newMax, scaleOnMaxChange, and a max decrease catches it.
